organizations.description: The Asian American Journalists Association at USC is an organization that promotes diversity and inclusion for Asian American Journalists at USC Annenberg School of Communication and Journalism.Committed to providing opportunities and support for Asian American students, both undergraduate and graduate, in the Greater Los Angeles Area. AAJA's mission aligns with the five aspects of a Trojan — Faithful, Skillful, Scholarly, Ambitious and Courageous. We are committed to bringing more people of color in newsrooms, hosting workshops, and providing leadership opportunities in the field of journalism and communication at USC.

activity.title: There’s something delightfully full-circle about building an AI search company and then seeing it show up in print. Andrew and I were featured in the first-ever edition of The Corgi Times under the headline “The GEO Experts.” We started AthenaHQ because the way people discover brands is changing. Ranking in traditional search is no longer the whole picture. Brands also need to know whether ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and Gemini mention them, cite them, and recommend them. That’s the problem we’re solving. AthenaHQ helps teams measure their visibility across AI answer engines, understand the sources shaping those answers, and turn those insights into a practical plan for earning more discoverability. I spend most days thinking about software, data, and how quickly AI search is evolving. So seeing our work reflected back in newsprint felt unexpectedly special. Software moves fast. A newspaper has a different kind of permanence, especially when it is issue number one. Big shoutout to Erika for writing the piece, and to The Corgi Times for including Andrew and me in the inaugural edition. You gave “The GEO Experts” a very literal page in the history books. AI search is the future. It looks pretty good in print, too. ...more ...more

The best growth move I’ve seen this year came from an insurance company’s coffee shop Quick context: Corgi is an AI insurance company, and I just visited their Corgi Cafe aka their 24/7 space for founders, builders, and engineers, open around the clock, every day, no closing hours. They started with 1 location in San Francisco’s Financial District. Now they’re expanding to Atlanta, London, and multiple NYC neighborhoods. they also run their own branded buses, free routes connecting people through the city, on top of running a cafe. An insurance company running a bus line…. They even print their own newspaper. An actual physical newspaper, at a time when most people don’t even remember the last one they held. it made me think about something Andrew Chen (GP, built a16z speedrun ) told me recently: growth is never static. If a big player can run the same play as you, it’s probably not worth running. The stuff that actually moves the needle usually looks weird or too small for the big guys to bother with! Corgi isn’t growing insurance by advertising insurance. They’re building physical spaces, free transit, and even print media, and letting the community do the rest. FYI, I was NOT expecting cafe culture to involve tech people randomly pitching ideas and investors coming up to hear what people are building, but that’s exactly what happened. There were literal meeting rooms inside the cafe!! Traditional growth keeps changing because the traditional playbook keeps getting crowded. The edge is in the stuff nobody thinks to try yet. What are some crazy growth/marketing ideas y’all have seen? 👇 ...more ...more

Erika Lee Brooke LeBlanc - we had an amazing marketing & sales onsite and I got to meet some of my favorite colleagues from all over (especially nyc). shout out to the pic of well deserved superlative winners Bao Phan & Brett Miller , (Thanks to all who voted for me on “big brain energy” 🥹- it’s wild to see how others perceive you vs self) - we launched Procurement. as someone who works on brand/content partnerships and is constantly in the app, this has been a game changer. - We welcomed Lulu Guan as our field events marketing manager to shape even more of our startup community and ecosystem - my remit has shifted to influencer and cultural activations, where we get to embrace WEIRD marketing more than ever in Silicon Valley. Erika Lee moved from Los Angeles to San Francisco because of a cold DM on X. She grew up in the LA suburbs, and after attending college there she built her career in journalism across the country, first covering local news, and then crypto. Then in February, the chief of staff at Corgi , the AI insurance startup that recently went viral for its seven-day workweek, messaged her on X to ask if she would be interested in a role. She'd never heard of Corgi, but she'd seen a lot of people in crypto pivot to the AI industry and wanted to check it out. A week later, she flew to San Francisco to visit the team, and in March, she joined them as their Head of Brand. Her entire life changed in an instant. Read about what she learned from her move on Business Insider : https://lnkd.in/e3tK6Aer (Credit: Courtesy of Erika Lee) #LosAngeles #SanFrancisco #AI #relocation ...more ...more

In SF, networking is everything. Maybe that's why offline events and physical spaces carry so much weight there. On my first business trip to SF, I visited Founders Cafe as a guest and got a glimpse of the founder scene. Over the following months, I watched Corgi Cafe take off. And on my latest trip, I saw the buzz around Cafe Cursor firsthand. So, this article started with a simple question: could I tie these places together as a single trend? Thank you Victoria Olaogun , Erika Lee , and Ben Lang for the generous interviews, and Brooke LeBlanc for her thoughtful written answers! Thanks also to Duha Higginson and Evan Buhler 亦凡 for helping with the outreach 🙏 ...more

Today, we’re announcing another A$11.5m at a A$115m valuation 🤖 Bringing our total raised to over A$16m. The round was led by Square Peg , with continued support from Blackbird Airtree , Skip Capital and an incredible group of angels, founders and leaders from Tesla , Waymo , OpenAI , Anthropic and more. The investor support means a lot. But the signal that gave me the confidence to raise again came from our customers. A full day of robot test analysis now takes ten minutes. At Advanced Navigation , that has helped the validation team go from two tests per week to ten. Questions that once took weeks can now be answered the same day. Results like these are why Alloy Robotics has raised again, barely one year after we started. 🚀 Since launching publicly late last year, we have deployed Alloy across agriculture, defence, drones, medical devices, industrial systems, maritime robotics and humanoids. And we have learned something important: Robotics teams are not short of data. They are short on memory. The context needed to understand a robot is scattered across logs, images, tickets, code and the heads of individual engineers. When something fails, teams piece that context together manually. When it happens again six months later, much of the investigation starts from scratch. Alloy gives robotics teams and AI agents a shared memory over the data their machines produce. We understand the robot as a complete system across hardware, firmware and software, then bring answers into the tools where engineers already work. The principle is simple: - Every run should make the next one better. - Every test should improve the next design decision. - Every firmware update should carry the context of past fixes and regressions. - Every support ticket should draw on what the fleet has already experienced. That is the compounding loop we are building. This capital lets us move faster: expanding globally, deepening our robotics-specific intelligence and evaluation capabilities, and investing further in implementation and support. Our investment in service and partnership has been our unfair advantage, so we’re doubling down. I’m incredibly proud of the small, deeply technical and customer-obsessed team we have built. And I’m deeply grateful to our partners Jethro Cohen , Tom Humphrey , Jackie Vullinghs and Olivia Sioud (Grivas) , our customers, and everyone who has backed us along the way. Raising capital is a means to an end. Helping teams build safer, better and more reliable machines is the goal. This is our life’s work: accelerating robotic intelligence and, ultimately, robotic abundance. If you’re building and deploying robots, I’d love to talk. If you want to help build this future, we’re hiring.
